Doom and Gloom: Overreactions to Utah’s slow start to the 2026-27 season

📅 2026-11-04  |  Read Source →

This has not gone as well as we had hoped. Seven games into the season, and all that the "winning time" Utah Jazz are bringing to show and tell is a solitary one-point win against a subpar New Orleans team and a head bowed in shame. It was a depressing show-and-tell presentation for this premature Jazz team.

But growing pains are part of the deal. Winning in the NBA isn't as simple as a change in mindset; it's a change in identity. A fundamental shift in the direction of a franchise will take time to set, especially one as drastic as going from hunting the number-one overall lottery odds to walking the thorn-riddled path toward the Western Conference playoffs.

Just as Michael Scott learned that it takes much more than shouting in the office to declare bankruptcy, Utah is learning firsthand that flipping the "winning" switch is much harder than simply making a declaration. The Jazz wanted and expected to win many more basketball games this season; they clearly still have some growing up to do before they can reach that switch.

Still, it wasn't ridiculous to expect more from this team by now. They traded for Jaren Jackson Jr., one of the best front-court defenders in basketball and a multiple-time All-Star, to pair alongside Utah's in-house All-Star, Lauri Markkanen. They drafted Darryn Peterson, a player touted as one of the best guard prospects in recent memory and a future star. They re-signed Keyonte George, rewarding him for his steady growth and remarkable leadership.

But 1-6 is 1-6, and the Utah Jazz are way off course at this larval moment in the 2026-27 season. Not all is lost, but much needs evaluation and careful reconsideration. So let's play a game that I like to call "Doom and Gloom". The rules are simple: I'll share an opinion that I've thought myself or heard from others about Utah's unsettling beginning and determine whether said opinion is "Doom", a bad omen and an imminent issue, or "Gloom", an overreaction that, while based in reality, doesn't tell the whole story.

SAN ANTONIO, TX – NOVEMBER 2: Ace Bailey #19 of the Utah Jazz drives to the basket during the game against the San Antonio Spurs on November 2, 2026 at Frost Bank Center in San Antonio, Texas. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and/or using this Photograph, user is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Adam Hagy/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images

No, the Utah Jazz are not winning basketball games. Yes, that is a massive problem, and a legitimate cause for concern for a team whose goal is to win basketball games.

But this problem, as with all others, deserves some context before it stirs up panic.

The biggest factor, I believe, is the Jazz's strength of competition. According to ESPN's RPI, the Jazz are tied at number-one for the hardest schedule in the entire NBA. They've faced the reigning Western Conference champions, San Antonio, twice while the Spurs were at full strength. Who could have foreseen the Memphis Grizzlies, who Utah faced twice, starting the season at 6-1? In fact, all the teams that beat the Jazz at this point of the season are a collective 22-6.

Despite the majority of this Jazz core having played together for years, this is a team still discovering itself. Give them time.

Injury luck has not flipped in Utah's favor early — five big men have been injured at some point in the season — but to blame their shortcomings on injuries is disingenuous.

Jusuf Nurkic hasn't been available since the first game of the preseason, Jaxon Hayes went down with an injury against Los Angeles, and then Markkanen and JJJ went down in the same half against Memphis. Markkanen and Hayes returned quickly, but shortly thereafter Mo Bamba — who has been unironically excellent — rolled his ankle in San Antonio.

That's bad luck, and Utah will obviously underperform without their best players on the court. But playoff-caliber teams regroup and find ways to win while shorthanded. If the Jazz can't win while JJJ recovers from his MCL injury, their playoff chances were slim from the start.

Alright, it's time for some therapeutic pessimism. On the topic of Utah's young players, I have to be painfully honest: Utah's tanking-fueled draft yield has been tragic.

Let's look at the Jazz's body of work in terms of draft picks. Of their four lottery picks, only two are still on Utah's roster. First to leave was Taylor Hendricks, who spends his days at the end of Memphis' bench and doesn't appear likely to sign an extension at the end of the season. It's a similar story for Cody Williams, who, despite generating plenty of preseason static in Minnesota, has appeared in five games and scored zero points.

Utah traded up to pick Florida star Walter Clayton Jr. last year, and he's already on his third NBA team.

As for the draftees still on Utah's roster, Isaiah Collier's team option was just declined, and Kyle Filipowski hardly sees the court even as injuries pile up in Will Hardy's frontcourt rotation.

Sensabaugh's minutes have been uneven, but he's filled his role well and had the trust of his head coach to replace Darryn Peterson in the lineup when their first clash with San Antonio entered overtime. Still, his status with the team is uncertain as he approaches the final year of his contract.

That list doesn't inspire much optimism, but it isn't all bad in terms of the youth of Utah.

Keyonte George has been excellent this year, with the exception of a stinker against San Antonio. Ace Bailey is a revelation, making winning plays with and without the basketball, playing stellar defense, and becoming an offensive rebound magnet. And Darryn Peterson, despite looking uneven out of the gate (more on this later), has still shown flashes of what makes him such an enticing prospect.

Semi-Doom is a bit of a cop-out, I'll admit. But there's still reason to believe in Utah's young core, even if the majority of their swings have inarguably whiffed.

Even worse than seeing Utah lose five consecutive games is seeing how the team has responded to adversity.

Without a rallying cry or an increased sense of urgency, this team is full of players with no experience winning at an NBA level. They haven't been able to hit that next gear, and the team mopes on the court, on the sideline, and in timeouts.

This is all about perception, so I might be out of line, but winners turn losing streaks into winning streaks. Utah is giving its fanbase little reason to expect a turnaround because they don't appear to expect one themselves.

Being a guard in the NBA is incredibly difficult, and development isn't linear.

What we're seeing in Peterson isn't a lack of basketball talent, ability, or confidence. In fact, he's displayed all three of those qualities in droves in his young career. Instead, we're observing the metamorphosis of a college star into an NBA-level player. Darryn Peterson joins a Utah Jazz team where he is the fourth offensive option behind Markkanen, George, and Jackson Jr. Finding his place in the rotation and getting accustomed to his new circumstances was bound to bring growing pains.

The biggest concern has been his lack of athletic burst and top-end speed, keeping him away from the basket. Instead, he's sustained himself on a diet of floaters and mid-range jumpers, while getting comfortable with a quick-trigger three-point shot.

For every poetic dribble combo leading into a buttery-smooth jumper, Peterson is due for a forced off-balance fling. He's playing in the big leagues, which means the competition is bigger, stronger, and faster than he's ever faced.

And I'm still highly encouraged by what he's displayed to this point. The jumper looks slick, comfortable, and will find its target with greater consistency over time. Keyonte was a sub-40% shooter from the field as a rookie; he shot 45.6% in his third year.

Alright, I'll wave the red flag for this one. Utah's offense has been abhorrent this season, and we can't blame tanking on their ratings anymore.

Currently possessing the 29th-ranked offense in the entire NBA, the Jazz have scored under 100 points in their last two games. Lauri Markkanen played in both of those games and has performed well beneath his standard. At just 16.5 points per game, the player who has been Utah's offensive pillar and averaged over 26 points per game a season ago is shooting below 40% from the field.

Against San Antonio on Monday, Markkanen and Peterson were the only Jazz players to score in double digits.

The absence of Jusuf Nurkic has been devastating to Will Hardy's offensive game plan. Heavily reliant on ball screens and passing from the center position, Jaxon Hayes simply isn't the playmaker this system requires to succeed. Nor are Mo Bamba or Tony Bradley.

Having to adjust on the fly, the Jazz offense has been clunky, ineffective, and overly dependent on self-creation to pose any real threat. Either one player's injury has truly been that catastrophic to Utah's offensive integrity, or Will Hardy is struggling to conjure up an alternative play style. Either way, none of this is good.

Calvin Barrett is the Associate Editor for SLC Dunk and a Utah Jazz columnist for the Standard-Examiner. Originally from Springville, Utah, he currently writes from his desk in Japan.

Jalen Brunson has a simple explanation for his surprisingly slow Knicks start

📅 2026-11-04  |  Read Source →

Jalen Brunson's field goal percentage (39.3 percent), 3-point percentage (33.3 percent) and free-throw percentage (73.2 percent) are all significantly down from last year. In fact, the field goal and 3-point percentage would represent the worst of his career, while the free-throw percentage would be second worst.

The Knicks captain has uncharacteristically been misfiring.

There isn't some deep-lying issue or explanation, though. Brunson believes it's actually quite simple.

"Missing shots," Brunson said after practice Tuesday, "I normally make."

New York Knicks guard Jalen Brunson reacts after making a 3-point shot against the Brooklyn Nets on Monday, Nov. 2, 2026, at Madison Square Garden in New York. JASON SZENES FOR NEW YORK POST

Brunson's shooting was always a worry after he underwent surgery to fix a tendon issue in his left wrist during the offseason. He spoke before the season about how it disrupted his normal offseason workouts and caused him to take way fewer shots than he normally does.

It is certainly understandable that there is early-season rust. But, true to his character, he refused to use that excuse.

"Not at all," Brunson said when asked how much the surgery has affected his early-season form.

His shot diet, in terms of the percentage of pullups vs. catch-and-shoot and shot distance, is similar to last season's. As are the percentages of open shots vs. tightly covered shots. This is not a case of worse shot quality leading to worse results.

There is one area in which there has been a big drop, though. He is struggling in what is usually his specialty.

Brunson's efficiency at the end of the shot clock is way down. He is shooting just 26.7 percent with between 7 and 4 seconds left on the shot clock and 35.7 percent with under four seconds left. Last year, he was at 48.8 percent with between 7 and 4 seconds left on the shot clock and 46.6 percent under four seconds left. Brunson bailing the Knicks out with tough shots late in possessions is usually a staple of their offense and something that demoralizes opposing defenses.

It's been part of a larger trend with the Knicks and their sluggish offense to start the year. As a team, they are shooting 30.4 percent from 7-to-4 seconds left in the shot clock and 26.5 percent under four seconds left. Those are the second-worst and worst marks in the NBA, respectively.

So often, as Brunson goes, the Knicks go. This is a clear example.

"He's taking the same shots as in the past," coach Mike Brown said Tuesday. "In my opinion, he's just missing shots. He's taking the right shots. I think all our guys are, for the most part, taking the right shots. Right now, they're not going in. And that can be for this reason, that reason, I don't know, and I'm not going to try to overanalyze it. As long as they keep taking the right shots, keep working on the shots, I think eventually they're gonna fall sooner than later."

Brown has coached some of the league's best-ever scorers, including LeBron James, Kobe Bryant and Stephen Curry. He has seen this before.

New York Knicks guard Jalen Brunson (11) shoots a three-pointer against the Brooklyn Nets at Madison Square Garden in New York, Monday, Nov. 2, 2026. Jason Szenes for NY Post

And he knows that usually, these ruts don't last too long.

"It happens," Brown said. "It happens to the best of them because everybody is definitely human and every human has their ups and their downs when it comes to shooting. That's why we have to keep embracing the little things, because they're not gonna always fall."

It's rare to see Brunson struggling the way he has to start this year.

But if he's taking the same shots as normal, it should be expected that the results will soon return to normal.

Lakers star Luka Dončić has second technical foul rescinded

📅 2026-11-04  |  Read Source →

Los Angeles Lakers star Luka Dončić has created a lot of attention this past week with his ability to score.

He's managed to produce a fast start for the Lakers and has positioned himself as an early candidate for MVP.

Dončić produced a double-double in a 138-117 victory over the Miami Heat at Crypto.com Arena on Nov. 2. He finished with 42 points, 13 assists and seven rebounds.

The point guard did receive a technical foul with 1:12 left in the second quarter. He was initially called for the technical foul for clapping in the direction of an official as he was disputing a "no-call."

It would've been his second technical foul of the season, but it was officially rescinded by the NBA on Tuesday. He will not have to pay the $2,000 fine.

"This season," Dončić told reporters on Oct. 21. "I'm trying to not get techs."

More: Luka Dončić's offense is carrying Lakers. Is LA too dependent on its 'showman'?

Dončić had received his first technical foul of the season during a game against the Golden State Warriors on Oct. 30.

If a player receives their 16th technical foul in a single season, they are automatically suspended for one game and fined $5,000.

Houston Rockets vs. Minnesota Timberwolves game preview

📅 2026-11-04  |  Read Source →

Last season, the three matchups between the Houston Rockets and Minnesota Timberwolves ended in a combined score of 350-351. None of the three were blowouts, as the largest margin of victory was Houston's lone win in the series (by 5 points).

The two losses were different levels of devastating, though. Both came towards the end of the season and basically tanked any chance Houston had of holding home court advantage in the first round of the playoffs. It turned out that not having those first two games in Houston really hurt since the Los Angeles Lakers rode the crowd to 326 TS%* over those first two games (*all stats are approximate but seriously the Lakers couldn't miss in Games 1 and 2).

The first loss was the one where Houston held a 13-point lead in overtime. It was easily one of the most impressive first two minutes of an overtime period I've ever seen. Then it was followed by the most devastating three-minute stretch in overtime, as Minny closed on a furious 15-0 run to win. It was yet another in a long list of late-game collapses for that Houston squad.

The T-Wolves come in without Anthony Edwards, who is recovering from arthroscopic knee surgery, but there was enough success early for proof-of-concept in the Ant-LaMelo Ball pairing. It definitely looks like they can work together, and the further ascension of Jaden McDaniels gives them enough cover for the two months waiting for Ant's return.

The Wolves also have this generation's Thaddeus Young in veteran Rockets killer Jonathan Kuminga. He's playing well this season so I expect another career night out of him against a team he always shows up to play.

15 players to watch amid NFL trade deadline buzz

📅 2026-11-04  |  Read Source →

Take a look at the NFL standings. There's no sure thing this season.

Once the Los Angeles Rams got off to a rocky start, it opened things up around the league. There is no runaway team this season, and there is also a group of teams already looking ahead to 2027. That could lead to a ton of activity before the NFL's trade deadline, which is on Nov. 10. There has been plenty of action well ahead of the deadline, with players like guard Quenton Nelson going to Seattle, defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons landing in Chicago, defensive tackle DeForest Buckner heading to San Francisco, cornerback Joey Porter Jr. being shipped to Dallas and receiver Marvin Harrison Jr. being dealt to Houston.

That's already a lot of big trades and we're just getting started. Here are the 15 names to watch between now and the deadline:

There was a quarterback change in Arizona on Sunday and it will stick. Brissett was removed late in the third quarter for Gardner Minshew, who led a wild comeback win over the Cowboys in overtime. The Cardinals announced Monday that Minshew will start Week 9 with rookie Carson Beck being the backup.

All of a sudden, the Cardinals have a third quarterback who could be moved. Minshew can handle the starting job as well as the struggling Brissett was doing, and Beck will get starts at some point. Teams don't usually trade their backup quarterback, but Brissett isn't even the backup anymore and is expendable. And he has plenty of starting experience, though his $15.5 million salary for this season would have to be managed to swing a deal with most teams. He's the most likely quarterback to move at the deadline for any team desperate for a stopgap starter (perhaps the Ravens?). – Frank Schwab

If we take the Browns at their reported word, Sanders is not likely to be traded at the deadline. You can never say never until the deadline passes, but for now it appears Cleveland will continue to carry four quarterbacks, which includes Sanders. He has been QB2 behind Deshaun Watson and has replaced Watson for a handful of snaps after Watson got hurt. Watson was sacked eight times Sunday, and the 5-3 Browns might fear a more serious Watson injury as they sit just outside the current playoff picture after Week 8's defeat to the Steelers.

Given his cost-controlled salary, low draft pedigree and Cleveland's crowded QB room, Sanders might normally be considered a higher-likelihood trade candidate. So far there has been little apparent traction. We'll see if that changes over the next week. Perhaps there's even a world where Sanders is in the mix to start in Cleveland if the free-agent-to-be Watson is not brought back in 2027. – Eric Edholm

The Eagles reportedly won't trade Barkley. That also doesn't make much sense. Philadelphia is going nowhere, Barkley is turning 30 years old in February, his production has declined since 2024 and the Eagles have never been overly sentimental about player moves. Barkley brought great memories and was the superstar on a Super Bowl champion, but the Eagles should listen to calls. They could pass if teams try to get Barkley cheap, given his current injuries, but it seems like he'd have more value to a contending team this season than the Eagles going forward.

Maybe the Eagles are serious and Barkley is indeed off the table. That won't stop speculation. It makes a ton of sense for Philadelphia to move Barkley now. That's why we're still keeping an eye on Barkley as the deadline approaches. If they don't move him, that decision will be discussed not only at the deadline but beyond. – Frank Schwab

It would be a surprise if Taylor isn't traded, after the Colts sent off guard Quenton Nelson and defensive tackle DeForest Buckner. The question is who lands Taylor and his 8,208 career rushing yards. He's still one of the NFL's best runners and plenty of teams have a need. The Giants, Broncos, Packers and Vikings top the list. While other backs are likely available, nobody else would pop like Taylor. Other players might be more prudent from a football aspect (Jeffery Simmons to the Bears, most notably) but no player acquisition would generate more buzz than nabbing Taylor. – Frank Schwab

Pollard has said he doesn't want to be traded, and the Titans reportedly have rebuffed offers, but a 1-7 record and a reasonable proposal could change their minds. He's in the final year of a three-year deal, makes fairly modest starting RB money and would provide the Titans with some salary cap relief if they moved him.

Pollard has averaged a robust 4.5 yards per carry, has back-to-back 100-yard rushing outings (and five TDs in two games) and remains in his relative prime at age 29 with fewer than 2,000 career touches. On paper, he checks every box for a sale candidate if the Titans want to add more draft assets before the deadline. And for teams looking for RB help, he might come far cheaper than some of the other players mentioned above. – Eric Edholm

The memories of Thomas' rookie season might last forever. They could lead to some team thinking it can revive his career. Thomas was a first-round draft pick in 2024 and had 1,282 yards and 10 touchdowns. He looked like a future star. In the season and a half since he has fewer than 1,000 yards. He has fallen well out of the Jaguars' hierarchy at receiver, leading to plenty of trade speculation. The Jaguars, who look like Super Bowl contenders, could keep Thomas just in case there are injuries at receiver. But teams like the Seahawks, Chiefs or Commanders would likely be interested, hoping Thomas rediscovers his rookie form in a new situation. – Frank Schwab

Interestingly, Jennings was rumored to be a target of the 49ers, trying to bring him back into the fold, but declined the offer, saying he didn't want to go back to San Francisco. That's especially interesting considering his best production came with the 49ers, notching a 975-yard season in 2024 and a nine-TD campaign a year ago before leaving on a one-year deal in Minnesota. Jennings has been almost a ghost with the Vikings, with only six catches in his six games and only modest upticks in his activity lately.

The Vikings need all the offense they can find, but Jennings hasn't been a great fit. If they can include him in a deal for a running back or defensive depth, the Vikings might consider it. – Eric Edholm

Downs has requested a trade, saying he's "open to whatever" when it comes to moving on from the Colts. The team has already kick-started its offloading efforts with Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner, and don't appear to have strong intentions to keep Downs. The 25-year-old receiver is in the final year of his rookie deal and has stepped up as the Colts' leading option with Alec Pierce hurt. Downs doesn't fit a WR1 profile but could be a quality complement for a team seeking an upgrade to its unit, similar to the Seahawks' deadline trade for Rashid Shaheed last year.

Downs is a smaller slot receiver and might be a fit for only certain teams, but with his trade request and the seeming league-wide need for WR help, he figures to be a candidate who possibly moves on soon. – Eric Edholm

Jeudy has always been mercurial. He came into the NFL as a first-round draft pick and was fine early on with the Broncos, but wore out his welcome and was traded to the Browns. With the Browns, he had a stellar 2024, with 1,229 yards and a Pro Bowl nod. But he has dipped again and with the Browns turning toward rookies Denzel Boston and KC Concepcion, Jeudy has just 171 yards this season. Still, Jeudy has one of the biggest plays of the Browns' 5-3 start, a 33-yard catch against the Ravens to set up a game-winning field goal.

Jeudy, 27, could be an intriguing gamble for a team that needs juice at receiver. He's no sure thing, but the talent is there. – Frank Schwab

Mack isn't the same player he was when he was a first-team All-Pro three times in four years. His peak might lead him to the Pro Football Hall of Fame. He's 35 years old now, but still is an effective player. And with the 0-7 Chargers going nowhere, it would make sense for the team to move on and allow Mack a chance at playoff success in what might be the final season of his career. Mack is in his 13th season and has never been part of a playoff win.

Mack would add leadership and a strong edge defender down the stretch for a contender. Mack has 8.5 sacks in 19 games over the past two seasons, including three in seven games this season. Given his age, he might not cost that much. A reunion with the Bears seems like the perfect fit. – Frank Schwab

When the Eagles drafted Smith in 2023, draft experts lost their minds. They gave the Eagles a consensus grade point average of 4.12 — better than an A. While the Eagles' first pick, defensive tackle Jalen Carter, worked out very well, Smith has not.

Smith has just 14.5 career sacks but still has the draft pedigree and enticing athleticism. The Eagles picked up Smith's fifth-year option for 2027, which means they won't be looking to give him away. But for a floundering Eagles team, the idea of recouping some value on Smith during his fourth lukewarm season has to be a possibility.

There are a lot of Eagles on this list. Philadelphia becomes the seller to watch as the trade deadline approaches. For some contender looking for a shot on a sleeper, taking a stab at Smith at age 25 could pay off nicely. – Frank Schwab

Sweat reportedly requested a trade in August, and the Cardinals very publicly said they had no interest in honoring that request. Could they have a different mindset now? Arizona has won two of three and is a fairly respectable 3-5, albeit in a very tough division the Cardinals are unlikely to win. Sweat's play has not been as impactful as a year ago, when he notched 12 sacks and four forced fumbles, but he had a huge sack in overtime of Dak Prescott in Dallas on Sunday.

Speaking of Dallas, the Cowboys figure to be among the teams that could have interest in Sweat, along with the Packers, where Jonathan Gannon (his former coach) is defensive coordinator. Sweat's contract kicks up to $23.6 million salary cap hits each of the next two seasons, which puts him outside the top-10 edge rusher deals, but there have been rumors of Sweat wanting a new deal after this season, which could complicate things. – Eric Edholm

There are conflicting reports on the 25-year-old Ojomo and whether the Eagles might consider dangling him. Normally, they'd want to build around an emerging defensive tackle who has started the past three games and been more productive recently than highly paid DTs Jalen Carter and Jordan Davis. But Ojomo is set to hit free agency, and it's unlikely the Eagles can afford him after what they paid Carter and Davis. If the Eagles have designs on re-signing Ojomo, they'll have to be creative. They are 2-6, losers of six straight, including back-to-back thumpings in prime time, and QB Jalen Hurts (along with others) is on injured reserve. The Jeffery Simmons trade to Chicago had to be an eye-opener for Philly, value-wise, and might cause the team to consider moving him before the deadline. – Eric Edholm

Baker has been tremendous for the Cardinals over his 10 seasons with the team, making eight Pro Bowls. But it might be time for a rebuilding club to move on. Baker can provide playmaking at secondary, as he has for a decade. He is signed through 2027, with a reasonable salary of a little more than $16 million for next season. So he wouldn't be a short-term rental for a team.

It would sting for the Cardinals to move on from Baker, one of the team's best players and only positive lights in the post-Larry Fitzgerald era. But it's prudent for a team looking for the future. And it would be a big get for a contending club that needs a difference maker in the secondary. – Frank Schwab

Following his three-pick game Sunday against Joe Burrow, Hooker is the NFL's INT leader with five, and his 114 return yards off those picks also is first. The 28-year-old veteran has quietly carved out a nice career over eight seasons with the Titans and is enjoying one of his better years, tackling and covering well. The Titans signed him to an extension last summer through the 2028 season with a fairly reasonable salary outside the top 10 safeties.

Given their 1-7 record at the bye, the Titans could offload more vets after trading Jeffery Simmons. – Eric Edholm

Buyers, sellers or fence-sitters? All 32 NFL teams slotted before the trade deadline

📅 2026-11-04  |  Read Source →

NFC East: Cowboys | Giants | Eagles | Commanders NFC North: Bears | Lions | Packers | Vikings NFC South: Falcons | Panthers | Saints | Buccaneers NFC West: Cardinals | Rams | 49ers | Seahawks

AFC East: Bills | Dolphins | Patriots | Jets AFC North: Ravens | Bengals | Browns | Steelers AFC South: Texans | Colts | Jaguars | Titans AFC West: Broncos | Chiefs | Raiders | Chargers

Where does your team sit as the NFL's trade deadline fast approaches?

Not all needy teams will swing trades prior to Nov. 10, but some certainly will look. On the other end of the spectrum, not all out-of-contention teams will hold fire sales, but with the recent spate of big names moving, there are opportunities to sell now and cash in later.

And, as we know, some teams will sit idly by as the deadline comes and goes. The NFL might be as active, trade-wise, as it has ever been in-season, but not every team is willing to pay the asking prices they're hearing.

Here's how we view all 32 teams, slotting each of them into one of three categories — buyers, fence-sitters and sellers — prior to the trade deadline. Teams are roughly ordered within each section by their perceived fits: strongest at the top, weakest at the bottom.

The Bills are the top seed in the AFC in spite of a defense that clearly needs help. Sunday's blowout of the Ravens notwithstanding, that unit isn't as likely to perform to that level against top-tiered quarterbacks and offenses. There are questions about how much the Bills want to give up in any prospective trade, and they're hamstrung a bit right now by salary-cap space (less than $4 million), but that can be rectified if needed. Safety might be the biggest position of need, although they also could look for extra pass-rush help.

Defensive tackle DaVon Hamilton suffered a torn quadriceps in Sunday's win over the Colts and will miss the rest of the season. It's hard to understate how big a blow this is. Head coach Liam Coen said the Jags will take a committee approach to replacing Hamilton, but finding a nose tackle is easier than finding other positions, so it would not be surprising to see them try to add a plugger up front. Safety is another spot they could consider. The Jaguars (5-2) are steamrolling toward a division title, and are in the hunt for the AFC's top seed. There's no better time to go for it.

They're already buyers after the DeForest Buckner trade, and they might not be done. They reportedly reached out to the Vikings about Jauan Jennings before they found out Jennings wasn't interested in a return. But receiver figures to be a position they consider upgrading, along with edge rusher and possibly cornerback. The 49ers have to be very cautious with Mike Evans; they've been a vastly better team with him on the field. Adding WR insurance, given all the injuries there, feels like a low-risk move that's on the table.

Their first buy of trade season, Jeffery Simmons, sunk his teeth into the Seahawks on Monday night. It's the kind of move that turned a very good team into a downright scary one. You can't blame the Bears if that's all general manager Ryan Poles gets done prior to the deadline, but the one area of concern coming out of the Seattle game had to be cornerback. Jaylon Johnson and Tyrique Stevenson both had rough nights with Malik Muhammad out, so we expect Poles to work the phones for CB help. They also could look for a pass-rush addition, with old friend Khalil Mack a name often bandied about these days. The Bears appear to be in Super Bowl mode now. They're out shopping.

The Vikings' offense could keep them from a Super Bowl, so they figure to seek help on that side of the ball — specifically a running back or an offensive guard. The run game has slowed down, and Aaron Jones Sr. has battled knee issues. The Vikings really could use more of a workhorse to complement Jones and Jordan Mason. They've also been connected to some pass rushers, scary as that sounds for opponents.

The Chiefs are stricken by limited salary cap space, but they figure to look and see what's out there. Wide receiver is the biggest area of concern — again — with Tyquan Thornton out for the season and Rashee Rice seemingly dealing with chronic soft-tissue issues. General manager Brett Veach has a decent history of smaller-to-medium deadline moves, so you can't rule anything out here. They also could mine for pass-rush help, but that might be tougher to find — and afford.

The primary need appears to be on defense, a unit that started strong but has tailed off. The Bengals could use help at multiple spots, although cornerback figures to be the most concerning, especially after watching Cam Ward pick them apart Sunday. A coverage linebacker and another pass rusher would be nice, too. On offense, if there's a need, it's at running back. They're averaging 3.7 yards per rush, with a long run of 15 yards this season.

Dallas is 3-5 yet still in the hunt for how poor the NFC East is. Team owner Jerry Jones says the Cowboys remain on the lookout for more help, and though they had been historically quiet at the trade deadline, Jones backed up his talk with last year's deadline deal for Quinnen Williams and the earlier-season trade for Joey Porter Jr. The Cowboys' defense is getting manhandled now. They badly need pass-rush help, but another corner would also be nice. Then again, so could more LB help. Jones said they won't want to flush more draft picks on a player who isn't under contract long term, but they might be desperate enough to add wherever they can.

The Patriots remain in contention at 5-3 (and a 3-0 mark in the division), but they could have concerns on both sides of the ball. On offense, they could use guard reinforcements after Alijah Vera-Tucker and Mike Onwenu landed on injured reserve. On defense, pass-rush help probably tops the list, but they also could seek LB and DB depth. Following the major A.J. Brown trade this summer, it would be surprising if the Patriots relinquished major draft assets. Any moves they make figure to be on the lower-compensation side, perhaps for a veteran's expiring contract.

Detroit fans have let general manager Brad Holmes know they want action prior to the deadline, especially after seeing the 49ers, Seahawks and Bears add starters last week. The Lions' defense is the biggest concern by far. The injuries to LBs Jack Campbell and Jimmy Rolder have left a big hole in the middle. Safety is in better shape with Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph back, but cornerback remains problematic. Pass-rush help also could be addressed. Can Holmes find the right help in the next week?

After adding Rashid Shaheed last year and Quenton Nelson this year, we know the Seahawks are open for business this time of year. Did Monday's home blowout loss to the Bears change their level of aggression? A struggling run game is an area the Seahawks could seek to help, although Zach Charbonnet's return could make them look elsewhere. They could try to add one more pass rusher and possibly another receiver for an offense that has been too JSN-dependent.

The Giants have found themselves atop the NFC East, and their first in-season trade for QB J.J. McCarthy has borne some early fruit. Could that move portend another (or others) if the Giants keep finding ways to win? Possibly. We know that John Harbaugh personally called Titans owner Amy Adams Strunk about Jeffery Simmons, but that call went to voicemail and Simmons went to Chicago. Defensive tackle figures to be the spot most likely to be addressed, but don't rule out a cheaper running back to stabilize that shakier position.

The Steelers already have been sellers, trading CB Joey Porter Jr. to the Cowboys. But sitting in first place in the AFC North in what's roundly expected to be Aaron Rodgers' final season, the Steelers might try to get back to buying. Not coincidentally, they could use a cornerback. Safety and wide receiver also could be spots they seek to upgrade. This doesn't feel like a team, however, that's prepared to go broke for that proverbial one final move.

They were close to being labeled "fence-sitters" after Sunday's breakout from RB Jonah Coleman. Running back had been the position that seemed most in need of being addressed prior to Coleman's big game Sunday. Now that feels like a luxury. Their most likely target position, if they try to swing a deal, figures to be offensive line or tight end.

This felt like an all-in season at one point, but that was before Myles Garrett and Davante Adams got hurt and the team started 2-4. The Rams have since evened their record at .500, but several tough games remain. The Rams certainly could be active, and another receiver certainly would help, but they've already depleted their trade assets significantly with the Garrett deal and don't have a ton to give up. They might want to add some help, but can the Rams realistically make an impact trade in time? It's unclear.

They've had some recent tailwind as a team, they've gotten Josh Jacobs back and Micah Parsons' return appears to be on the horizon. They also have some possible needs, including cornerback, if they can find the right trade partner. On the other hand, they've just been so historically quiet around the deadline under GM Brian Gutekunst (they actually have been more deadline sellers than anything), that I wonder if they'll do much.

The Texans have already bought, adding WR Marvin Harrison Jr., but is more coming? There are questions in the offensive and defensive backfields, and they continue to struggle to get the offensive line fully right. All those spots are possible. But the Texans are 2-5 and falling farther behind the first-place Jaguars. If Houston makes a move, expect it to be more on the minor end.

How seriously are the Browns taking their 5-3 start, especially after the humbling loss to first-place Pittsburgh? There are plenty of areas they could address, ample draft assets to part with and a general manager in Andrew Berry who has been among the most active in-season traders. But if the Browns don't feel this team has a legitimate chance to make playoff noise, they might be wise to keep their assets and load up more in the offseason. Browns fans would be giddy at a deadline deal, but patience might be preferred.

The Raiders feel like they are in no-man's land. They pulled back to .500 after losing four straight, but is Vegas capable of contending? The big drama now feels like when the Raiders will move off of Kirk Cousins and give the reins to Fernando Mendoza. There might be a case for the Raiders as sellers, with Cousins perhaps an intriguing piece for a team such as the Ravens that recently lost its starting QB. Other possible trade figures include Jackson Powers-Johnson and Adam Butler, but it also feels like the Raiders could ride things out without any major transactions the rest of the way.

The Panthers are a strange team to handicap. Carolina has clear needs, but at 3-4, with two straight losses, is it in position to add help? Oh, and did we mention that record puts the Panthers in first place? The playoffs are still very much a possibility, but this team being one or two moves away from being a Super Bowl contender is a stretch. If the Panthers add somewhere, cornerback feels like the most likely spot. Anything they do likely would have to be more than just a short-term rental at retail price.

Most of the NFC South profiles similarly to Carolina. There's a real shot at winning the division, but at what cost? There's also the chance the Bucs could look to sell, with names such as Yaya Diaby, A'Shawn Robinson and Chris Godwin Jr. being floated. But GM Jason Licht has not made an in-season trade since Tom Brady was QB, and it feels like the chances are greater that the Bucs do nothing.

They're 3-5 and 1-2 in the division, yet Atlanta has enough explosive potential offensively to be potential buyers. Even after Michael Penix Jr.'s four-INT game, the Falcons might think they have a real shot of taking the division. The receiver depth is light, and there are still holes to patch on defense, although they might treat the return of James Pearce Jr. from suspension as their big pre-deadline addition.

I'd put the Saints more in the "sellers" bin, sitting at 2-5 with team owner Gayle Benson already having aired her grievances with the team's performance publicly. A loss to the Browns this weekend might push them closer to moving some pieces. The question is about what players might be available and sought by other teams. If another team wanted Alvin Kamara or Cameron Jordan, the Saints would almost have to sell. Otherwise, there just aren't a lot of tradable assets that might tempt other teams.

The Jets certainly could be sellers, with the season again slipping away and the focus continuing to shift to what could be one of the franchise's biggest offseasons, armed with three first-round draft picks — with all three currently in the top 10. Adding to that should be a consideration. Garrett Wilson and Breece Hall are two big names that could be on the move, but to this point they've publicly pushed back against dealing either. If they are active, I expect lower-profile pieces such as Harrison Phillips or Nahshon Wright to be more likely than the bigger names.

The Commanders kept their season alive in the watered-down NFC East with a win over the Eagles on Sunday night, and there's a chance they could be lighter buyers if they can find a running back who fits their short- and long-term vision. They also could be sellers, with pass rusher K'Lavon Chaisson the most logical piece to try to move. It's hard to get a clear read on what GM Adam Peters wants to do, but he said he's talked to all 31 teams and continues to work the phones.

The Colts have already sold off two major assets in Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner. There's not much stopping them from continuing to put other players up for sale. WR Josh Downs has reportedly requested a trade and figures to be in play in the coming days. RB Jonathan Taylor might cost too much to be moved before the deadline, but the Colts are acting like a team just waiting for a bigger offer to pull the trigger. Lacking a first-round pick in 2027, the Colts need all the draft-pick help they can get.

For years, GM Howie Roseman has been about the most aggressive talent hunter out there come deadline time. This season, following a string of poor developments and six straight losses, the Eagles look far more like sellers on the outside. There is no shortage of players the Eagles could move. They have several expiring-contract candidates, including TE Dallas Goedert, CB Riq Woolen, WR Marquise Brown, DT Moro Ojomo and others. There also are players under contract beyond 2026 who could be available, including OG Landon Dickerson and Edge Nolan Smith. They've already made one trade and could be open for more business with this season apparently shot.

The Chargers have continued to hoard assets for now, but as the league's final winless team, it's worth wondering what they're waiting for. GM Joe Hortiz was turning away calls at one point because the team believed a turnaround was coming. It was not. If they finally become sellers, Khalil Mack figures to be an easy piece to move — a veteran pass rusher on an expiring deal. Teams seeking nose tackle help should probably call on Dalvin Tomlinson. WR Quentin Johnston also could be available if the team doesn't think he can reach his ceiling there. There are deals to be made if the Chargers shift their thinking.

The Dolphins are not making the playoffs this year, although it's reasonable to be encouraged by their competitiveness. Still, this is a sell-off phase for the Dolphins if they can cook up some interest in players such as Zach Sieler, Austin Jackson, Josh Uche or others. The problem is that Miami's roster is already so heavily loaded with rookies and minimum-salary players that there are only so many assets to move. But the Dolphins gladly will vacuum up any draft picks other teams are willing to fork over in this multiyear rebuild.

Shipping out well-liked Jeffery Simmons was a sign that the Titans are in sell-now mode. RB Tony Pollard is probably their most tradable piece, but it's not clear if they want to move him. Anyone can have WR Calvin Ridley for a song, if they want. Edge Jermaine Johnson II also might be a name you hear this week after picking him up from the Jets this offseason. Dinamo Zagreb under the lights at the Stadium of Light on Bonfire Night.

Last season's surprise Premier League package are rooted to the bottom of the table, with just one win and six defeats from nine games.

Will a game against the champions of Croatia on Thursday (20:00 GMT) serve as a welcome distraction before Sunday's visit of Chelsea?

When Sunderland won at Stamford Bridge last season in their ninth game back after promotion, the Black Cats sat second in the table after an electrifying start.

After nine games this season, it is a very different story.

Questions are being asked about the long-term future of manager Regis le Bris - the man who masterminded Sunderland's return to Europe for the first time in 53 years.

So after last season's impressive seventh-placed finish, why are Sunderland struggling this time round?

Following last Saturday's 3-1 defeat at Coventry City, captain Granit Xhaka questioned the team's "courage", weeks after France defender Nordi Mukiele claimed the side had become "arrogant".

BBC Sport understands Le Bris' job is not in immediate danger and he will be given more time to turn things around.

The Frenchman, in charge since July 2024, is Sunderland's longest-serving manager since Steve Bruce, who was in charge between June 2009 and November 2011.

Le Bris has credit in the bank for winning promotion and then claiming a European spot.

This season he has managed to propel the Black Cats into the Carabao Cup quarter-finals, where they face fellow Premier League strugglers Crystal Palace at Selhurst Park.

But how long will Sunderland's hierarchy remain patient if the club, two points from safety, stay anchored in the bottom three?

"They ended last season quite well to get into Europe and that felt really historic," former Sunderland loan signing Nedum Onuoha told BBC Sport.

"But there was talk then that maybe he [Le Bris] wasn't quite the guy.

"Sunderland fans who probably had their doubts last season, I really doubt that they will be thinking he is the manager long term."

French football expert Julien Laurens added about former Lorient boss Le Bris: "This is not looking good.

"I look at Sunderland and I'm not seeing him find the solutions to turn things around. For me that is really worrying."

Sunderland's paradox - San Siro trip amid relegation battle

Sunderland's only Premier League win this season was on 30 August, a 1-0 victory at home to Fulham [Getty Images]

Sunderland, who were playing in League One as recently as 2022, were lauded as one of the stories of last season, after doing the double over Chelsea and fierce rivals Newcastle, as well as holding both Arsenal and Manchester City at home.

The numbers suggest repeated success was always going to be difficult.

Only relegated Burnley and Wolves had a lower Expected Goals difference - comparing the amount of good chances created to those chances created against them - than Sunderland last campaign.

How about that dreaded second-season syndrome then. Is it even a thing?

Last season Sunderland and Leeds became the 53rd and 54th promoted sides to survive in the Premier League.

Of the previous 52, only 11 were relegated the following season (21%). The vast majority of promoted teams that stay up do not suffer from second-season syndrome.

With three-quarters of the Premier League season to go, Sunderland will rightly argue there is plenty of time to save themselves.

Yet those heady days of 12 months ago must feel a long way off.

Two of Sunderland's seven league goals this season have come from the penalty spot, while they have finished with 10 men in defeats by Arsenal (Reinildo Mandava sent off), Bournemouth (Kevin Danso sent off) and Coventry (Omar Alderete sent off).

Meanwhile, Sunderland have failed to score a first-half goal in seven of their nine league games.

"Having been promoted many will have believed Sunderland exceeded expectations by finishing in the European places last season," added Onuoha, who made 31 Premier League appearances for the club in 2010-11.

"This season it is five points from nine games with seven goals scored. That speaks for itself in some ways - especially when three of those seven goals came in one game [a 3-5 defeat at Manchester City].

"It doesn't feel at the minute that things are heading in the right direction."

Where is it all going wrong for Sunderland?

Sunderland spent £161m on 15 new players after winning promotion to the Premier League in the summer of 2025.

This time round, just £60m was invested on five players.

Most fans, however, will have been delighted to keep hold of experienced captain Xhaka and forward Brian Brobbey, who scored seven league goals last season before going on to score three for the Netherlands at the World Cup.

Brobbey, who has signed a new contract until 2031, has yet to score since returning from a hamstring injury, while former Arsenal midfielder Xhaka was downbeat after last weekend's defeat at newly promoted Coventry.

"I don't know exactly what the problem is," said the Switzerland midfielder.

"Is it concentration? Is it other things? We are bottom of the league but in football you need to think positive and to show courage as well.

Carl Jenkinson, who was at Arsenal with Xhaka, told BBC Sport his former team-mate's remarks were "concerning".

"He seemed really deflated and that is very unlike Granit," added the former full-back, who made 41 Premier League appearances for the Gunners between 2011 and 2019.

Laurens said the form of Xhaka and Mukiele, who helped Sunderland towards 11 clean sheets in the top flight last season, had dipped significantly this season.

"They are the leaders and they are way below the levels they had," he added. "The first one to pay the price [for the team's poor form] is usually the manager."

Sunderland are without a win in seven Premier League games [Reuters]

For many, the reason for Sunderland's current struggles appears obvious - the added demand of Europe.

Their first European campaign since 1973 means at least eight games in the Europa League. Unlike in the Premier League, Sunderland have started well in Europe, winning two and drawing one of their first three league phase matches.

"Europe is great," added Laurens. "Sunderland fans will be travelling to Milan, it's wonderful.

"It could be a distraction for the players - especially the ones who have never played in Europe before. It's less time to practise on the training pitch.

"You play Thursday-Sunday and that's a very different dynamic to what Sunderland had last season."

Sunderland have lost two and drawn one of their three Premier League games after playing in Europe.

They could certainly do with beating Chelsea on Sunday after playing Dinamo Zagreb to lift the mood.

Otherwise it is going to be an unhappy international break for Sunderland and their passionate fanbase.

Man City could face further charges as Premier League confronted with ‘dilemma’

📅 2026-11-04  |  Read Source →

An increasing number of English football executives are pushing for the Premier League to investigate Manchester City for the seasons since 2018 or bring further charges, although it is a subject causing significant debate and viewed as a potential "dilemma" for the game.

The Abu Dhabi-owned club were last month found guilty of 114 charges of breaches of financial rules in a case already seen as one of the most controversial in football history, although they are currently in the process of appeal.

Amid a temporary lull in the story as the game waits for both the sanctions and the outcome of that appeal, many directors have been pointing to key details of the independent commission's final verdict.

Manchester City are appealing after being found guilty of breaching Premier League financial rules (Getty)

Since the document laid out how City's sponsorship deals were inflated by disguised owner investment, with accompanying graphs, an obvious question being asked is whether that just stopped in 2018, despite commercial income accounted as staying at the same level.

As one source asked, "what changed overnight?"

In its decision, the Independent Commission found that Manchester City and its Abu Dhabi-based sponsors were 'Related Parties'. If the relationships did not change, then that would form the basis for more charges in subsequent seasons given the club did not report this or have the Fair Market Values of the sponsorships assessed.

Opposition fans have delighted in City being found guilty of 114 charges (Reuters)

The ultimate reason for the initial investigation was a tranche of emails from football leaks that were first published by Der Spiegel in November 2018 and covered the period from 2009 to 2018.

While even those who want scrutiny on that period have concerns about another lengthy investigation, the wait for sanctions – expected by many sources to come this month – has sharpened focus on the period after 2018.

There is at least some possibility that the independent commission recommends titles of 2012, 2014 and 2018 are stripped. While this is currently viewed as unlikely, such an outcome would immediately raise more questions about the era of success that followed 2018.

City built on Pep Guardiola's initial 2017-18 title winning season with the most intense period of glory the Premier League has seen, winning English football's first four in a row to make it a total of six leagues in seven years alongside a first ever domestic treble and the 2022-23 treble that brought the Champions League.

Executives feel that questions about this have not been adequately addressed by the Premier League, although the competition's policy and legal guidance has been to refuse to discuss the case until it is completely concluded.

Pep Guardiola and Abu Dhabi helped build a sustained period of success at Man City (Getty)

The Premier League have been contacted for comment by The Independent.

There is nevertheless a sense among executives that commercial deals after 2018 will be viewed as having simply been made subject to the associated party rules, and were already assessed at fair market value.

That line of thinking has been met with some scepticism, given the nature of the guilty verdict.

The counter-argument is that associated party rules would be irrelevant here, since any investigation would be about disguised funding.

City are still strenuously insisting on their innocence, and remain bullish about an appeal.

Man City strenuously upon insist on their innocence and are bullish about their appeal (Getty)

The prospect of further investigation is also seen as representing a potential "dilemma" for the competition and its clubs. Some feel agitating executives are getting ahead of themselves, and that there should just be patience for the current case to conclude.

A concurrent view is that there aren't the same clear grounds for another investigation without evidence like the leaked emails, and that it might even be unnecessary if the guilty verdict is upheld and the sanctions are appropriate, given what the final verdict already says.

The latter is taken to mean meaningful sporting sanctions and focus on the hierarchy responsible.

Others feel the idea of another investigation is better saved as a "negotiation tactic", especially with how abrasive City have already been in their position.

Some feel another prospective investigation could be used as a 'negotiation tactic', especially if Khaldoon Al Mubarak (pictured) and Abu Dhabi are forced to sell City by the Independent Football Regulator (Getty)

As one source said of the guilty verdict prospectively being upheld, "when you're seeking to agree on a potentially severe punishment, the Premier League can be shown to have given them a concession and spare them further".

"It is pressure useful for the end game," another added.

That could also be acutely relevant to the future of the club if this case does conclude with a forced sale under the Independent Football Regulator, or even a voluntary sale, which certain rival executives are mindful of. Any agreement not to investigate further would ensure that potential buyers are not put off by the possibility of further uncertainty and more sanctions.

Some fear that another investigation would take another half-decade or more, and that the Premier League would suffer further when many are keen to eventually draw a line under the case.

One of the greatest players in Tampa Bay Lightning history may soon be wearing a different jersey. According to Sportsnet, Nikita Kucherov has told the Lightning he won't sign a contract extension and has requested a trade.

Kucherov, a two-time Stanley Cup champion and two-time Hart Trophy winner as league MVP, is one of the best players of his era. The 33-year-old just passed the legendary Steven Stamkos for the all-time franchise lead in points and has shown no signs of slowing down.

Just last season, Kucherov posted 44 goals and 86 assists en route to his second Hart Trophy win. His underlying numbers were even better with a five-on-five goal differential of plus-38 and an expected goals share of 57.0 percent. Only a select few players can drive play from the wing like Kucherov, and that makes him a unicorn of sorts.

Kucherov is in the final year of a contract that pays him $9.5 million per season, and with the salary cap rising rapidly, he's due for a gargantuan raise next summer. It sounds like Kucherov and the Lightning were too far apart on that number, so the superstar winger has shifted his focuse to a change of scenery.

It's important to note that Kucherov has limited trade protection in the form of a 10-team trade list, but that should be more than enough for the Lightning to find a suitable trade partner. With that in mind, let's take a look at five teams that would be ideal fits for Kucherov as he prepares for the next chapter of his illustrious career.

Right out of the gate, this is the most natural fit of all the potential landing spots. General manager Kent Hughes has done a superb job of locking down his young core on team-friendly contracts, and as a result, the Canadiens have nearly $30 million in projected cap space for next season. They also have a glaring need in their top two lines, and I'd say the reigning Hart Trophy winner would fill that role quite nicely.

Montreal's moment to strike is now. It's an ascendant team with a great salary cap situtation and assets to spend. It's time to make a splash, and this would be a tsunami. Just imagine Kucherov on a power play unit with Nick Suzuki, Cole Caufield, Lane Hutson and Ivan Demidov. Kucherov would also be coached by former Lightning teammate Martin St. Louis, so a rapport would already exist between player and coach. I expect the Canadiens to do everything in their power to land Kucherov.

We already know the Wild are big-game hunting at forward because they've been heavily linked to former Detroit Red Wings captain Dylan Larkin. If I were advising general manager Bill Guerin -- and I'm certainly not -- I would recommend Minnesota package whatever assets it has offered Detroit and redirect them to Tampa Bay. No, Kucherov is not a center,  and that's the Wild's biggest need.

However, Kucherov is a rare breed of winger in that he can drive play better than most first-line centers from the wing. Put him on a line with Kirill Kaprizov, and the only time opponents will touch the puck is when they're pulling out of the net.

With Quinn Hughes also on an expiring contract, acquiring Kucherov would be a risky move for the Wild. What if they give up premium assets only to lose Kucherov and Hughes next summer? I don't think fear can dictate Minnesota's decisions. The team has a top-two defenseman in the world on its roster right now, and it has the opportunity to acquire a top-five forward. Worry about next summer when the time comes. Go all in to win the Cup while you have a chance.

Carolina has a good chunk of cap space available already, and it wouldn't need to shed much in order to make room for Kucherov. Why MLB could see an early free agency frenzy before the potential Dec. 1 lockout

📅 2026-11-04  |  Read Source →

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Most of the season, my assumption was that November would be a slow month for the hot stove. There is a new collective bargaining agreement coming, likely after a lockout, and I figured teams would not want to commit significantly to future payroll without first seeing what the new CBA would bring. Salary cap, stiffer competitive balance tax penalties, whatever.

A perfectly reasonable stance, that is, and I say that as someone who is happy to call out teams and owners who do not appear to be putting forth the best effort to contend, if you catch my drift. My assumption was November would be slow. I am here now to tell you why my assumption not just may be wrong, but likely is wrong, and the hot stove will burn bright in November.

The CBA expires at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1, or four weeks from Tuesday. Here now are four reasons why MLB clubs could be active between now and then.

MLB teams committed more than $1.7 billion to free agents in November 2021, just before the last CBA expired and the owners locked out the players. That includes the Rangers, who spent more than $560 million on Jon Gray, Corey Seager, and Marcus Semien. Those three later helped the Rangers win the franchise's first World Series title in 2023. Five players signed nine-figure contracts in the weeks leading up to the last lockout.

It is not only the teams we must consider here. More than 140 players became free agents the day after the World Series, and you can be sure many (most?) of them would prefer to sign before the lockout. They want to get their contract locked in and know where they'll play next season so they can find a place to live, get the kids enrolled in school, etc. Peace of mind during the lockout will go a long way.

MLB's owners did not propose a salary cap during the last round of labor negotiations, but there was similar uncertainty about what the upcoming CBA would bring, and teams spent lots of money anyway. Past behavior can inform us about what to expect in the future and what we saw leading into the last lockout suggests it will be a busy four weeks.

During the last lockout, MLB amended its posting agreement with Japan's Nippon Professional Baseball league and paused the 45-day negotiating window during the lockout. Seiya Suzuki was posted on Nov. 22, 2021, his 45 days were paused when the lockout began on Dec. 1, then they resumed when the lockout ended on March 10, 2022. Suzuki signed with the Cubs on March 18.

NPB players will not have the same luxury this year. MLB has declined to amend its posting agreement this offseason, according to The Athletic, so NPB players potentially face a hard Dec. 1 signing deadline even though they were officially posted on Nov. 1. They won't get the full 45 days because players cannot sign MLB contracts during the lockout. Their posting window is really 30 days.

This applies to three of our top 50 free agents: Hanshin Tigers third baseman Teruaki Sato (No. 4), Seibu Lions righty Kaima Taira (No. 19), and Hokkaido Nippon Ham Fighters righty Hiromi Itoh (No. 26). All three were posted on Nov. 1 and their 45-day posting window should run through Dec. 16. Instead, they must sign by Dec. 1 with the lockout looming, or return to Japan for 2027.

Tarik Skubal, far and away the best free agent on the market, is expected to sign before the lockout, reports ESPN. There is always a bit of a domino effect with top free agents. Several big spenders (Blue Jays, Cubs, Dodgers, Mets, etc.) are expected to pursue Skubal, and the teams that lose out could quickly pivot to their secondary targets to avoid being left empty-handed.

We saw a good example of this domino effect last offseason. The Dodgers beat out the Mets for Kyle Tucker and agreed to terms with the outfielder on Jan. 16. The Mets quickly pivoted and agreed to a contract with Bo Bichette just a few hours later. They had money to spend and a void in the lineup, and after losing out on their top target, New York quickly pivoted to Plan B.

The sooner Skubal signs, the sooner second-tier free agent starters like Freddy Peralta and Trevor Rogers will come off the board. Teams need pitching, always and forever, and once the best available starter comes off the board, there figures to be a rush to get whoever's left. Skubal is expected to sign before the lockout. Other starters won't be far behind then.

Even if the MLB Players Association relents and agrees to a salary cap, it is unlikely the cap will be fully implemented in 2027. MLB has expressed a willingness to phase in a salary cap over some number of years and, honestly, it's a must. It will be impossible for big payroll clubs like the Dodgers, Mets, and Yankees to trim payroll and get cap-compliant immediately after the lockout.

November may be the last chance for all teams, not just those with deep pockets, to spend freely and have contracts grandfathered into whatever economic system the new CBA brings. Spend now, deal with the consequences later. That kind of thing. It may sound foolish -- the bill will come due eventually, right? -- but rarely is the hot stove league and free agency rational.

"You prepare under the current system, and then you adjust along the way," Blue Jays president Mark Shapiro told Sportsnet last month. "Any new system adopted, there will be a timeframe for adjustment into that system. I don't think any new system adopted would cause for immediate action."

Mariners hire Cubs executive with no managerial experience as new manager

After a colossally disappointing 2026 season, the Seattle Mariners are bringing in a first-time manager. The Mariners have named Chicago Cubs director of player development Jason Kanzler their new manager, the team announced Tuesday. Seattle fired manager Dan Wilson after the season.

"Our goal in this process was finding a manager with the ability to challenge all of us to improve," president of baseball operations Jerry Dipoto said in a statement. "Jason has the mindset, expertise, communication skills, and intensity to help create a championship standard here in Seattle."

The Mariners will be Kanzler's first managerial job at any level. At 36, he will be the second-youngest manager in baseball, older than only 34-year-old Washington Nationals skipper Blake Butera.

Bringing in a manager with zero previous managerial experience at any level is a rare move, certainly, though it is not unprecedented. Most notably, the New York Yankees hired Aaron Boone straight from the broadcasting booth in 2018. Boone had no managerial or coaching experience at any level. He's led the Yankees to the postseason eight times in nine seasons.

"I am thrilled to join the Mariners organization and I'm looking forward to hitting the ground running," Kanzler said in a statement. "This team has an immense amount of talent in all facets of the game, and my coaching staff and I are excited to access and unlock this team's full potential."

Kanzler may have no prior managerial experience, but this will not be his first time on a big-league staff. He was a major-league coach with the Houston Astros in 2022 and their assistant hitting coach in 2023, and had coached in their farm system previously. The Cubs hired Kanzler to oversee their player development in 2024.

Former Astros manager Joe Espada was reportedly the other finalist for the Mariners job.

The Mariners went 76-86 this past season and finished five games back in the woebegone AL West. A year ago, they went to Game 7 of the ALCS and were five outs away from their first-ever trip to the World Series. Seattle entered 2026 as a trendy World Series pick and instead fell flat, mostly because so many core hitters underperformed.

Kanzler will be the team's third manager since Dipoto was hired to run baseball operations in September 2015, joining Scott Servais (2015-24) and Wilson (2024-26).
